text: His appointment as CEO led to a turnaround.
The restructuring of the company took two years.
His decision to start a doctorate surprised his colleagues.
After the sale of the company, he returned to law.
During his tenure, the company doubled its revenue.

Every year we receive more than three hundred speaker bios, and most of them have the same problem. They are lists. Born in, studied at, worked at, worked at, worked at. Nobody reads a list. A good bio tells a short story with a clear line. Start with what the speaker does today, not with the university. Then choose two or three moments that explain the career: an appointment, a turnaround, a difficult decision. Write them as events, not as a sequence of verbs. For example, instead of he was appointed CEO and he restructured the company, write: his appointment as CEO led to the restructuring of the company. It is shorter, and it sounds more professional. And please, keep it under one hundred words.

People always ask me why I left a career as a CEO to go back to law. The short answer is that I missed the questions more than the answers. During my tenure as CEO, the company went through a difficult turnaround. We sold two businesses and rebuilt the rest. It was a great experience, but I realized that the part I enjoyed most was the regulatory side: the negotiations with the agencies, the drafting of the rules. So after the sale of the company, I made the decision to return to practice. I also started my doctorate, which was a dream from my university years. Looking back, the transition was the best decision of my career.
